# Conventions every work skill follows

Every skill in the work plugin follows these rules. A skill's own `SKILL.md`
names the file when a rule matters for a step.

This file is `references/conventions.md` in the work plugin's own folder. From
a skill's `SKILL.md` it is two folders up: `skills/work-on/SKILL.md` and
`references/conventions.md` share the plugin folder. In Codex the plugin
folder is the installed copy, for example
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/`, so this file is
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/references/conventions.md`.

Four rules that are easy to miss:

- Run each `toolkit` command alone, as its own command (below).
- Never change a work item with a script (Python, Node, `sed -i`, `cat >`).
  Use `toolkit work edit --section` or `--label`, or the file edit tool for
  body text. The hooks refuse the script, so it only wastes a step.
- Temporary text goes in `--text`, or in a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder,
  never at a fixed name such as `/tmp/wi001.md`.
- End every reply to the owner with the one question he must answer, or with
  the exact words that continue the work ("Say 'keep going' and I'll start the
  build."). Never end on "The next step is ..." with nothing for him to do.

## Voice

Every skill carries this line near its top:

> Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

Agents do not receive the output style. Each agent file in `agents/` carries
its own writing rules.

## Opening another skill

- Claude Code: use the Skill tool with the skill's name, for example
  `work-requirements`.
- Codex: read that skill's `SKILL.md` from the path shown in the skill list,
  then follow it.
- Say the handover in one line, for example "WI-012 needs a design; opening
  solution-design."
- The skill that asked a question records the answer. An answer that arrives
  later, after that skill has finished, is recorded by `work-decide`.

## Running `toolkit` commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command.
  Do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a pipe, or a redirect. Codex matches its
  command rule against the plain command. This holds for read commands too:
  `toolkit work decisions && toolkit work show WI-001` is two commands.
- In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion,
  Hindsight, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and `.memory/` from a
  worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong cause. Run each one
  alone, as its own command.
- Add `--json` when you need to read the output field by field.
- Exit codes: `0` done; `1` error; `2` validation failure (fix what it names
  and run it again); `3` not supported for this tracker or memory backend
  (follow [trackers.md](trackers.md)); `4` not a Toolkit V2 project (open
  `project-setup`).
- "saved but not verified" in the output means the write happened and the
  read-back failed. The message names the first line that differs. Lead the
  reply to the owner with "Saved but not verified", say which line, and read
  the item back to judge it.

## Changing a work item

- Change a work item only through `toolkit work` commands. This keeps the
  local tracker and Notion the same, and it keeps the CLI's record of what it
  wrote. A value the agent changes by hand looks like an owner edit to the
  CLI.
- Find a file only with the command below. Never build a path by hand: the
  owner may have moved or renamed the folder.

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --path
  ```

- To change one section of the body, read it, change only what needs to
  change, and write the whole section back. The file holds the same text the
  read printed for that heading, with your changes.

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --section "<heading>"
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --set-file <file>
  ```

- To add one row to a table section (Open Questions, Recent History), use
  `--append-row` with the full Markdown table row. A new question takes the
  next free `Q-` number: read the Open Questions section first and add one to
  the highest number there (`Q-01` when there is none).

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row "| <next Q-id> | <question> | R-02 | Open | owner |"
  ```

- Frontmatter values change only through `toolkit work set`, `approve`,
  `design`, `move`, `finish`, and `cancel`. Never edit frontmatter by hand.
- A title is the owner's call. A new item's title uses the owner's own words
  for the request. When you shorten them or choose another, say the title in
  one line in the reply ("I started WI-003, 'Write a short project brief'.").
  To retitle an item, say the new title to him in one line before
  `toolkit work set <id> --title`, and never retitle an item quietly.
- Never hand-edit `.work-items/DASHBOARD.md` or
  `.work-items/.toolkit-state.json`. The hooks refuse it.
- Text for a section or a design:
  - Short or medium text, in both hosts: give it in the command with
    `--text "<text>"`. No file is needed, and newlines inside the quotes are
    kept:

    ```text
    toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --text "<text>"
    toolkit work design <id> --text "<text>" --status proposed
    ```

  - Claude Code, for long text: pass it on standard input, so no file is left
    anywhere: `toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --set-file - <<'EOF'`,
    then the text, then `EOF`. (In Codex a heredoc runs the command inside the
    sandbox; use `--text` or a file there.)
  - Codex, for text too long for `--text`: make a new folder for this one save
    with `mktemp -d` (its name is unique, so two sessions or two projects never
    share a file), write the file in it with the file edit tool, run the
    `toolkit` command alone with the file's full path, and delete the file and
    the folder right after the command succeeds (`rm <file>`, then
    `rmdir <folder>`), before you ask the owner anything. Never use a fixed
    name such as `/tmp/wi001-requirements.md`: every project starts at
    `WI-001`, so another session's save could land in this item. Never write
    the file and run the `toolkit` command in one shell command.
  - Never leave draft files inside `.work-items/`: a second `DESIGN.md`-shaped
    file there confuses the design lookup.
- Never write a work item record from the shell (`cat >`, `tee`, `sed -i`,
  `cp`, or a script) and never change its frontmatter with a file edit. The
  hooks refuse both, because they would skip the approval gates.

## Section names in `WORK-ITEM.md`

These are the headings `--section` uses. Every tracker uses the same body: the
project's `.work-items/work-item-template/WORK-ITEM.md`, copied from the model
project.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `Overview` | Goal, Current position, Next action (and who owns it), Blockers, Related items (ids, never paths) |
| `Roadmap` | Phases `P1`, `P2` with Outcome, Status, Exit result, Sub-items |
| `Tasks` | Tasks `P1-T01` with Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on |
| `Recent History` | Dated rows: change or decision, effect on the work |
| `Open Questions` | `Q-01` rows: question, affects, status, decision needed from (`owner` for the owner) |
| `Requirements` | Overall status, Starting request, Agreed goal, Active requirements `R-01`, Acceptance |
| `Notes` | Decisions and context, Resume here, Solution options and considerations |

The frontmatter fields are `id`, `title`, `type`, `stage`, `status`, `parent`,
`waiting_on`, `priority`, `delivery`, `requirements_approved`, `design`,
`result_approved`, and `updated`. Only `toolkit work` commands change them.

## Section names in `DESIGN.md`

The design has one shape in every tracker (`DESIGN.md` beside a local item,
the "Solution Design" page in Notion, the "Solution design" comment in GitHub
or Jira). The CLI writes its frontmatter: `work_item`, `status` (`proposed`,
`approved`, `superseded`), and `approved`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Header lines | Requirements (the item id), Design status, Requirements checked, Last updated, Design approval |
| `What this design solves` | Who uses the result, what they need, what must be true afterward, and what the design leaves to another item |
| `Requirements and design readiness` | One row per `R-xx`: its status in the item, the design coverage, and the remaining decision or gap |
| `What exists today` | Verified current behavior and files, or "nothing exists yet" |
| `Constraints and assumptions` | One row each, with source, status, and effect on the design |
| `Design options` | `### Option A — <name>` (then B, C) with Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage (Build or reuse, Why it meets the requirement, How to check it), Technical shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order |
| `Option comparison` | Only with more than one option |
| `Recommendation and owner decision` | Recommendation, Owner decision, Reason for decision |
| `Selected design` | After the owner chooses: End-to-end flow, Components and responsibilities, Data, access, and integration details, Edge cases and failure behavior, Release and ongoing operation |
| `Diagrams` | Mermaid diagrams, each with a heading and a one-sentence explanation |
| `Build and verification plan` | Technical sequence, and Acceptance checks (one row per requirement) |
| `Sources and decisions that affect the build` | Claim or decision, source, date, evidence type, how it was checked |
| `Where a builder could misread this design` | Requirement or section, plausible wrong reading, intended reading |
| `Notes` | Open design questions, Design changes during the interview, Current position and next step |

Keep the headings exactly as the template has them, including the dash in
`Option A — <name>`.

## Saving what the owner says

Save each settled answer in its home before moving to the next topic. An
unanswered question is also information to save. Open decisions do not delay
saving answers that are already settled.

| Information | Home | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirement or correction | The item's `Requirements` section (the `R-xx` block and Acceptance) | The new meaning, and Status `Refining` until approved |
| Design choice | The item's design (`toolkit work design`) | The approach, proposed or approved, and why |
| Open question | The item's `Open Questions` table | Question, what it affects, Open, who must answer (`owner` or a name) |
| Answer or decision about this item | The existing question row, the affected section, and one history note | The answer, who gave it, the date, and whether it is an approval |
| Decision for the whole project | `DECISIONS.md`, through `work-decide` | Decision, why, who decided, what it replaces |
| Outstanding task | The item's `Tasks` section | Work, deliverable, done when, depends on |
| Useful context that is not a requirement | `Notes` > `Decisions and context` | Only what the next session needs |
| Build idea kept for later | `Notes` > `Solution options and considerations` | The idea and the `R-xx` it relates to; it is not a requirement |
| A lasting fact, preference, or lesson | Project memory, through `memory-save` | One record |

- Check the item and memory before asking the owner a question again.
- When sources disagree, keep the conflict open and ask. Do not pick the
  convenient answer.
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer, or a saved draft is not
  approval. `toolkit work lifecycle` prints what counts as approval.
- Read the section back after saving. A command that exits `0` is not proof
  by itself.

## Reporting a failed save

- A write failed: lead with "Not saved", name what was not saved and where it
  should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- The write worked and the read-back failed: lead with "Saved but not
  verified".
- Never say "updated" first and correct it later in the same reply.

## When to add a history note

Add one `toolkit work history <id> --note "<text>" --effect "<what it changes>"`
when (without `--effect`, the row says which skill continues the item):

- the stage, type, priority, `waiting_on`, blockers, or next action changes
  for a reason that is not obvious;
- the owner gives a choice, an answer, a requirement, a constraint, an
  approval, or a rejection (quote his words);
- someone outside reports an approval (record who, and do not claim you
  checked it);
- a discovery changes the plan;
- a requested result is finished.

Record the owner's meaning briefly. Do not add reasons, scope, or certainty he
did not give. Do not log routine commands, files opened, ordinary test runs,
or small edits.

## Waiting on the owner

- Set `waiting_on` to `owner` when you ask the owner for an approval or add an
  Open Questions row that he must answer.
- `toolkit work approve` sets `waiting_on` from `owner` to `none`, because the
  owner just answered. After the approval, set it to `agent` when the agent
  continues. After the owner answers his last open question on the item, set
  it back the same way: `agent` when the agent can continue, `none` when
  nothing waits. Keep `owner` only while another question for him on that
  item is still open.

  ```text
  toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent
  ```

- An item left at `owner` stays in the briefing and in
  `toolkit work decisions`, and `work-on` sends it to `work-decide` instead of
  its next stage.

## Stages in plain words

- Show a stage with the item id and the plain label from
  `toolkit work lifecycle`, for example "WI-012 is in testing (stage 09)".
- Never ask the owner which stage an item is in. Work it out from the record.
- Status follows the stage. `waiting_on` shows who the item is waiting for.
  Blocked is not a status.

## Owner edits win

The owner may edit the tracker by hand: move a folder, drag a Notion card,
change a stage. The CLI keeps his value, adds a "Changed by hand" history row,
and reports it. Never undo it. When a hand change skips a gate (a build item
moved past stage 03 without approved requirements, or Done without a recorded
result approval), ask the owner about it as a question.

The session briefing lists these changes under "Changes found in the
tracker", and every `toolkit work` command prints the ones it finds. Tell the
owner each one in one line ("You renamed WI-002's folder to help-option; I'll
use the new path.") before other work. The CLI writes the history rows for a
hand move itself: "Moved by hand", "Folder renamed by hand", or "Parent
changed in Notion by hand" on the item, and "Sub-item ... moved out" or
"moved here" on the parents it left and joined. Add a note only for what the
CLI cannot know, such as the owner's reason.

## Branches and worktrees

- An item's code work happens in its own worktree
  `.claude/worktrees/wi-<number>-<slug>` on the branch
  `claude/wi-<number>-<slug>`, the form the project's
  `shared-repository-work.md` rule uses:
  `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export`.
  The briefing ties a worktree to its item by the item id in the branch name.
  With another id prefix, use it in lower case (`acme-007-...`).
- Never commit `.work-items/` or `.memory/`. They are Git-ignored and live in
  the main checkout.
- No AI credit anywhere: not in commits, pull requests, comments, or files.
- Codex: its sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only, so `git add`, `git commit`,
  `git worktree add` and `remove`, `git merge`, `git branch -d`, `git fetch`,
  and `git push` cannot run inside it. The project's
  `.codex/rules/toolkit.rules` makes Codex ask the owner before each one.
  - Run each Git write as its own command and ask for escalated permissions:
    set `sandbox_permissions` to `require_escalated`, with a one-line reason
    that says what the command does ("Create the worktree for WI-002 on its own
    branch."). An approval without escalation still runs the command inside
    the sandbox, where it fails on `.git/index.lock`.
  - Tell the owner in one line what the command does before Codex asks.
  - Codex refused it without asking ("approval required by policy, but
    AskForApproval is set to Never"): this session cannot ask. Stop that
    step, show the owner the exact command, ask him to approve it in an
    interactive session or to run it in a terminal, and set the item waiting
    on the owner. It is not an outside blocker.
  - Never work around it: no nested `git clone` of the project, no copy of
    `.git/`, no building on the default branch instead of the item's branch.
- The project's shared-repository rule runs `git fetch origin` before the
  first edit. When `git remote` prints nothing, the project has no remote:
  skip the fetch.
- A merge that stops on a conflict: resolve it, then commit with a message you
  write (`git commit -m "Merge <branch>: <what it brings>"`), never
  `git commit --no-edit`, which keeps Git's "# Conflicts:" lines in the
  message.
# Trackers

A project has exactly one tracker. `.toolkit.json` names it in
`tracker.type`. Read it with:

```text
toolkit config get tracker.type
```

| `tracker.type` | Where items live | How skills work with it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local` | `.work-items/` in the main checkout, one folder per item | `toolkit work ...` commands |
| `notion` | The project's own Work Items database in Notion, under the "AI Agent Second Brain" page | `toolkit work ...` commands (the CLI calls Notion) |
| `github` | GitHub Issues in the project's repository | Written instructions: [trackers/github.md](trackers/github.md) |
| `jira` | Jira issues in the project's Jira project | Written instructions: [trackers/jira.md](trackers/jira.md) |

## Rules for every tracker

- The same model everywhere: the fourteen stages, the six statuses, the
  `WORK-ITEM.md` body, and one design per item. `toolkit work lifecycle`
  prints the stages, statuses, types, and approval gates.
- Never create a second tracker, and never keep a local copy of items that
  live in Notion, GitHub, or Jira.
- A sub-item is its own item with its own requirements, design, roadmap,
  and approvals. Finishing a sub-item never finishes or approves its parent.
- Only the main agent changes a work item. Agents return findings; the main
  agent saves them.
- Read every change back.

## Local and Notion

- Every read and write goes through `toolkit work ...`. The commands behave
  the same for both.
- Local: a folder nested inside an item's folder is a sub-item. A plain folder
  with no record in it is a group. `archive/` hides items from the briefing
  and from `toolkit work next`. The project's rule for this tracker is
  `.claude/rules/work-item-folders.md`.
- Notion: the design is the item's "Solution Design" child page. A card the
  owner made with Notion's New button has no template body; the CLI fills it
  on its next read and reports it. A Stage the owner changed by dragging is
  kept, and Status follows it.
- Writes outside the "AI Agent Second Brain" page are refused by the CLI.
  Never work around that.

## GitHub Issues and Jira

- `toolkit work` commands exit with code 3 and print the path of the written
  instructions. Follow those instructions instead.
- The work-item hooks do nothing for these trackers, so the skill must keep
  the item correct by itself: read it back after every change.
- Create nothing in GitHub or Jira that setup did not already approve (labels,
  fields, workflows). Creating and updating issues for work items is part of
  normal work once the tracker was chosen.

## Templates for every tracker

The templates come from the model project. The toolkit plugin carries an exact
copy of the model in its `scaffold/model/` folder, so every project can reach
them, whatever its tracker:

- `scaffold/model/.work-items/work-item-template/WORK-ITEM.md`: the work item
  body. A new GitHub issue body or Jira description starts from it, from
  `## Overview` to the end.
- `scaffold/model/.work-items/work-item-template/DESIGN.md`: the design. A new
  design comment starts from it, without its frontmatter.

The file `~/.config/toolkit-v2/plugin-root` holds the path of the toolkit
plugin's folder (every session start refreshes it). The `scaffold/model/`
folder is inside that folder. A local project also has its own copies in
`.work-items/work-item-template/`, which the CLI prefers, so a project that
edited its template keeps its version. Both files open with a fill-in guide
comment: follow it, then delete it.

## What exists today

`README.md` calls this a tiny Node.js command-line tool that greets people. The repository has no CLI source, `package.json`, or implemented tests. Node.js v25.8.1 is available in this session. No Git remote is configured.

## Design options

### Option A — Read the version from package.json

#### Approach

Create `package.json` with `"version": "0.1.0"`. Create `bin/greet.js` as a CommonJS script that reads `require('../package.json').version`. The package field is the only version source. Node.js can read the JSON directly, so no package installation is needed.

#### End-to-end behavior

1. A person runs `node bin/greet.js` with a name, no name, or `--version`.
2. The script checks `process.argv.slice(2)` for an argument exactly equal to `--version`. If present, it prints the version from `package.json` and ends. Otherwise, it prints a greeting for the first argument or `world`.
3. The person receives one line on standard output. The five approved commands print the exact lines in the acceptance table below.

- **Access and security:** The command reads its own package file and writes text to standard output. It does not evaluate an input name or pass it to a shell.
- **Integrations:** Node.js CommonJS JSON loading, `process.argv`, standard output, `node:test`, and `child_process.spawnSync`; no external service.
- **Operations:** Run `node bin/greet.js` directly. Change the `package.json` version field for a future version. Keep `package.json` beside `bin/` so the relative read path remains valid.

A sub-item whose "Design:" says "none of its own" and names its parent's approved design is checked against that design: read the parent's.

2. Run the project's tests and every acceptance check the item lists. A check with several scenarios or manual steps gets a test plan: a copy of `tests/TEST-PLAN-TEMPLATE.md` named for the item, with the results filled in. A check that could not run is reported as not run, never as passed.
3. Brief the `acceptance-checker` agent (never the agent that built it): one verdict per requirement (met, partly met, not met) with evidence, plus defects seen in the diff. Give it the branch and commit to check.
4. Failures: set the bug-fixing stage; a `builder` agent (or the main agent) fixes; the checker checks again. Repeat until clean, or until a failure needs an owner decision (an Open Questions row and the item waiting on the owner).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 10-bug-fixing`
5. Record the result: what was checked, the evidence, the known gaps.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Checked: <what>; evidence: <where>; gaps: <gaps or none>"`
6. Set the approval stage and wait on the owner. Show him what it does now, how to see it (a link, a command, or a screenshot), the evidence, and the gaps. Ask one line: "Do you approve this result?"

# Acceptance checker

Check whether a finished result does what the owner asked. You are never the
agent that built it. You run tests and read code, but you change nothing. You
advise; the main agent fixes; the owner approves.

## Start with the brief

- The brief gives the work item id, the requirements (Agreed goal, every
  `R-xx` with its acceptance check, the Acceptance list), the design's
  Acceptance checks table (in its "Build and verification plan") and the
  "How to check it" column of the selected option's Requirement coverage, the
  item's test plan when it has one (a copy of `tests/TEST-PLAN-TEMPLATE.md`),
  the branch or commit to check, and the project's test commands.
- Check that you are looking at the exact code the brief names:

  ```text
  git status
  git rev-parse HEAD
  git log --oneline -5
  ```

  If the commit differs from the one in the brief, say so first.
- When the brief asks for a check before a merge, report the exact commit
  you checked, so the main agent can confirm nothing changed after it.

## Check

- Run the project's tests and every acceptance check you can run. Copy each
  command and its result line exactly.
- For each requirement, give one verdict:
  - **Met:** the acceptance check passed, or the evidence shows the required
    behavior. Name the evidence.
  - **Partly met:** some of the behavior works. Say what is missing.
  - **Not met:** the behavior is missing or wrong. Say what you saw.
  - **Not run:** the check could not run here. Say why and what would run it.
    Never report a check that did not run as passed.
- Read the diff for the item's branch against its base. Report defects you
  see: broken edge cases, missing error handling the requirements ask for,
  behavior the requirements did not ask for, files changed that the design
  did not name, and anything that would ship something unfinished.
- Walk the flow start to finish as the person who uses the result. Report any
  step where it breaks, even when each requirement passes on its own.

## Plan check (only when the brief asks for one)

Before a build starts, the brief may give the item's Roadmap and Tasks, the
requirements, and the design's "Build and verification plan" instead of a
finished result.
Then check the plan, not code:

- Every `R-xx` is covered by at least one task, and every task's "Done when"
  names evidence someone else can check.
- Each task has one owner, and each file has one writer. "Depends on" is
  right: no task starts before what it needs.
- Tasks that run at the same time have clear boundaries: no two builders
  write the same file, and no two use the same shared environment (a sandbox
  org, a database, a test service) at the same time without a stated order.
- No task relies on something the design or the code no longer says.
- Changes that affect other work items are named.

A different phase structure is not a defect by itself. Work that runs in
parallel does not need one agent per phase. Return for a plan check: the
verdict (ready to build, or not ready) in one line, then each finding with
the task id, what is wrong, and the fix in one line.

## Boundaries

- Bash is for tests and read-only commands only: running tests, `git status`,
  `git diff`, `git log`, `git show`, listing files. Never edit, stage, commit,
  push, merge, deploy, install, or delete anything.
- Never run a command against a shared or production org or service. Never
  touch production data.
- Never run a `toolkit` command that writes. Do not edit the work item.
- Do not start other agents. Do not ask the owner anything.

## Return (result check)

1. **Verdict:** ready for the owner, or not ready, in one line, with the
   commit checked.
2. **Per requirement:** a table with the `R-xx`, the verdict, and the evidence
   or the gap in one line.
3. **Tests run:** each command and its exact result line.
4. **Defects in the diff:** each with the file and line, what is wrong, and
   the fix in one line. "None found" when there are none.
5. **Not run:** each check that could not run, and why.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every file, function, and setting.
Short sentences, one idea each. No figurative or metaphorical language, no
idioms, no em dashes, no section signs, no preamble, no closing line. Keep
every number, path, and command output exactly as found. Lead with the
verdict and keep the report short. Never add a line crediting an AI.

# Local project memory

Keep future sessions oriented without turning every conversation into lasting memory. This folder is the project's built-in memory store and can be opened directly as an Obsidian vault. Active topics stay flat; filenames and YAML types agree. Git ignores this folder, so back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>`.

## Read and route

- Read `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` at startup; the session briefing includes it. Read `MEMORY.md` as a short index, then open relevant topics. Check dates, scope, and the current source before acting on a remembered claim.
- Read `memory-criteria.md` before selecting or changing memory. It holds the default eligibility rules; the `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy and the onboarding or trusted mode. Use the terminology glossary for project language, including distinct meanings across systems.
- Link related notes inside this vault with relative Markdown links, such as `[account model](project_account_model.md)`. Obsidian shows backlinks to a note from the notes that link to it; a second reverse link is optional. Link only when the relationship helps retrieval, and check that the target exists. Keep tracker URLs and paths outside `.memory/` as source references rather than vault links.
- Keep current tasks and owner-mentioned to-dos in `CURRENT_FOCUS.md`, naming work items by ID. Keep full tasks, status, requirements, history, and the work item's design together in the chosen tracker; verified system behavior in the System Guide; procedures in instructions or skills; and raw outside sources in their source folders.

## Curate

- Use a coherent topic file such as `project_account_data_model.md`. Allowed prefixes and matching `metadata.type` values are `user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, and `event`. `project_topic_template.md` is a seed, not a saved memory. Keep one related topic per file and aim for a quick read.
- Record source and date, status, scope, the durable point, why it matters, and how to apply it. Keep uncertainty explicit. Preserve extra YAML fields written by a host or imported record.
- Search for an existing topic before creating one (`toolkit memory find`). Correct, merge, or supersede in place where possible. Mark obsolete claims in both file text and index; do not leave an archived item reading as currently open.
- When renaming, merging, archiving, or deleting a topic, inspect links from other memory notes and repair any affected links, saving each repaired note with `toolkit memory save`. Do not leave a link pointing at a former active location.
- `toolkit memory save`, `retire`, and `restore` rebuild `MEMORY.md`; run `toolkit memory reindex` after any other topic change. The index holds one short link per active topic, not the content itself. Keep it below the configured budget.
- Keep `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` under 50 lines by replacing stale sections, not appending, and write it with `toolkit memory focus --set-file`. Do not remove an unresolved owner to-do solely to meet that limit.
- Keep the glossary broad through sourced real terms, aliases, and system-specific meanings, and write it with `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. Do not invent definitions.

## Authority and completion

- Save through the `memory-save` skill, which holds the approval policy for onboarding and trusted mode. An explicit request to remember or correct is authorization for that specific change.
- Ask before ambiguous, bulk, or irreversible deletion of unique content. Only the owner can change the mode.
- A rejected candidate is not saved to another memory, a criteria example, the glossary, or a pending queue. Record only the general selection lesson, as a `feedback` memory, if the owner gave one.
- The main agent writes this folder only with `toolkit memory` commands (`save`, `retire`, `restore`, `delete`, `focus`, `glossary`, `reindex`). They lock the folder, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index. Never run parallel writers against the same topic.
- Read back changes with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor` before reporting success. Memory work does not edit requirements, work-item status, designs, deployments, or source code.
# Memory criteria

This file is the project-specific selection policy: what is worth keeping in lasting memory. The approval policy, including onboarding and trusted mode, is in the `memory-save` skill, which saves with `toolkit memory save`. When the owner corrects what is worth saving, save the correction as a `feedback` memory with `memory-save`, as a general rule, without copying the rejected memory. Those `feedback` memories override this page.

## Default test for lasting memory

Save a topic when it concerns this project, has a credible source, would matter in a future session, would be costly or unreliable to reconstruct, and has no better maintained owner. Prefer updating an existing topic. A short pointer to an authoritative record can qualify when future sessions would otherwise miss that record.

| Type and filename | Usually worth retaining | Route or reject instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user_<topic>.md` | Relevant role, responsibility, working preference, or communication need the owner stated | Personal judgments, irrelevant biography, private details |
| `feedback_<topic>.md` | Repeated or standing correction to how the agent should work; confirmed selection lesson | One-off irritation, a rejected fact restated as policy, an instruction already in `AGENTS.md` |
| `project_<topic>.md` | Durable project constraint, rationale, technical landmark, or proven costly fix | A decision for the whole project (`DECISIONS.md`), code summary, schema copy, active ticket status, accepted requirement or design body |
| `reference_<topic>.md` | Hard-to-rediscover route to a source, system, dashboard, or decision record, with why to open it | Entire outside page or a path already obvious in `PROJECT.md` or the project map |
| `event_<topic>.md` | Significant project episode: what was done, what resulted, and where the output lives | Routine edit, tool call, raw error, daily progress log |

## Working context is different

`CURRENT_FOCUS.md` holds what is happening now: active work item IDs, what waits on the owner with no work item, untracked to-dos, and where the next session starts. It can change often. Keep a work item's detailed tasks and status in that item. Do not turn every open task into lasting memory. Do not discard an unresolved owner to-do merely to shorten the file.

## Never save as lasting memory

- Secrets, credentials, sensitive personal data, transcripts, scratch reasoning, raw logs, dropped guesses, or unsupported claims.
- A fact the same change already places in the authoritative file, unless a small route to that file is genuinely needed.
- Live status, pending approval, unshipped requirements, procedure steps, code restatements, or a current-system explanation that the code/System Guide owns.
- A rejected candidate under a new name or wider wording. A rejection stands until the owner changes it.

## Backup

This folder is Git-ignored. Back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>` and restore a fresh clone with `toolkit memory import --from <that folder>`. Linked worktrees resolve to one vault in the main checkout. A fresh clone or machine needs its memory restored before the agent treats an empty index as evidence that no memory exists.

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Record format, types, focus, and glossary: `references/record-format.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Put each `toolkit` command on its own line. In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a heredoc) or run from a script runs inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight and Notion: run it alone. Text: give it in the command with `--body "<text>"` (a save) or `--text "<text>"` (the focus or the glossary), so no file is needed. For a long text, in Claude Code pass it on standard input (`--set-file -` or `--body-file -` with a heredoc); in Codex make a new folder for each save with `mktemp -d`, write the file there, and delete the file and the folder right after the command succeeds. Never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/focus.md`: another session could write the same file.

## Steps

1. Decide the home first, with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory; otherwise `references/record-format.md`). Memory holds a lasting preference, correction, fact about the project or the owner, or a hard-to-find reference. Elsewhere: project work goes to `work-on`; a decision for the whole project to `work-decide` (`DECISIONS.md`); delivered behavior to `requirements/`; how a change is built to the item's design; verified current structure to `system-guide/`; outside documentation to `ai-external-knowledge/`; a standing rule for how agents work here is proposed as a rule-file change; an owner to-do with no work item goes to the current focus "Untracked to-dos"; a project term goes to the glossary. A short memory pointer to a hard-to-find record is allowed; never copy its body.
2. Search first and update the existing record rather than add a duplicate.
   `toolkit memory find "<topic>"`
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
3. Approval. This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy. Read the mode, then apply it:
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
   The owner's own words ("remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", a correction) are the approval: save now, with his name as the approver. `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first ("Save to memory: <one-line summary>?"); save after a yes. `trusted` mode: routine facts the agent is sure of are saved and reported, without an approver. Always ask first, in either mode, for anything about a named person, personal details, a hard delete, more than five records at once, or a change to this policy. A yes covers only the change and meaning shown. Silence is never a yes. There is no proposal inbox: keep an unanswered question in the conversation and go on with other work.
4. Save: type (`user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, `event`), slug, one-line description, the source, and a body file with the model's labels: Remember, Why (the owner's reason in his words, or "Not stated by the owner."; never a reason you inferred), How to apply, Evidence and limits (the source and an absolute date), Related memories (relative links such as `[deploy window](project_deploy_window.md)`), Authoritative records. The source is the person, conversation, or document the fact came from, with an absolute date, for example "The owner, in chat, 2026-09-26" or "requirements/billing.md, 2026-09-26". Saving the same type and slug again updates that record. Replacing a record under a new name: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. Giving the same record a better name, or a type that matches its content: rename it; links to it are repaired. Use the first save form when the owner approved (his words or his yes); the second only for a routine save in `trusted` mode.
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description "<one line>" --body-file <file> --source "<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>" --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description "<one line>" --body-file <file> --source "<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>"`
   `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`
5. "Forget that": retire the record (it can be undone); right after a save, retire that record with no question. Delete only when the owner says delete, and quote his words.
   `toolkit memory retire <key>`
   `toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved`
6. Focus and to-dos: read the current focus, change it, write it back. The model's format: a "Last updated" line (date, source, who) and four sections, under 50 lines, work item ids only, never their status. On a new project the focus still holds the setup text: remove the fill-in guide comment, and write "None." in each section that still holds only an angle-bracket prompt. Glossary terms the same way, sourced, never invented.
   `toolkit memory focus`
   `toolkit memory focus --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit memory glossary`
   `toolkit memory glossary --set-file <file>`
7. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): save it, then offer that change too.
8. Read the save back and check memory, then tell the owner in one line: "Saved to memory: <title>. Say 'forget that' to undo." A failed save is reported first as "Not saved". Never store work-item status, secrets, or email addresses.
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
   `toolkit doctor`

## Changing the approval mode

- Only the owner switches modes, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Silence, time, or many approved saves never switch it.
- Switch to trusted, or back to onboarding:
  `toolkit config set memory.approval trusted`
  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`
- Save his words as a `feedback` record with the date.

## Hook reminders

- The UserPromptSubmit hook adds a line when the owner's message contains a keep phrase ("remember that", "from now on", "note that"). It is a reminder, not an instruction to save everything: route it with step 1.
- The Stop hook blocks once when a keep phrase had no save this turn. Save it, or tell the owner in one line why it belongs elsewhere and where it went.

## Declined saves

- When the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Do not put the rejected fact in the current focus, the glossary, or another record. If his words give a general rule about what to save, save only that rule, as a `feedback` record.
- Several independent things can be grouped into one save. Never run two saves against the same record or the index at once.

## Backend notes

- Built-in `.memory/`: never edit the files by hand; the CLI writes them and rebuilds `.memory/MEMORY.md`. The folder opens as an Obsidian vault. When a record is renamed, merged, retired, or deleted, the CLI repairs the links in other notes and names each note it changed; read that report (`references/record-format.md`, "Links between memories").
- Hindsight or Notion unreachable: the save fails with "Not saved". Keep the text, tell the owner in one line, and retry later in the session.
